Dear Requester

Thank you for your request for an internal review of FOI 2026-020 concerning furniture, furnishings, antiques, fixtures, heirlooms and other movable property originating from Great House Farm (Ty Mawr), Llandough.

The reviewer has considered your original request, the responses provided by the Museum, the additional enquiries undertaken following your request for clarification on 3rd August 2026, and the concerns raised in your email requesting an internal review.

We are satisfied that the request was interpreted correctly and that reasonable and proportionate searches were undertaken to identify information falling within the scope of the request. Following the original response, the Museum undertook additional enquiries across relevant collections records and archived electronic records in order to satisfy itself that no information had been overlooked.

We are satisfied that the searches undertaken were appropriate to the nature and scope of the request and that no further searches are required in order to determine whether Amgueddfa Cymru holds information within scope.  The review therefore upholds the original decision that Amgueddfa Cymru does not hold recorded information concerning furniture, furnishings, antiques, fixtures, heirlooms or other movable property originating from Great House Farm (Ty Mawr), Llandough falling within categories 1 to 9 of your request.

Response to the points raised

1. Information identified concerning Great House Farm
During the additional enquiries, a small number of records referring generally to Great House Farm, Llandough were identified. These records do not relate to furniture, furnishings, antiques, fixtures, heirlooms or other movable property originating from Great House Farm and do not fall within categories 1 to 9 of your original request. The reviewer is therefore satisfied that they fall outside the scope of the request.

2. Scope of the archived electronic search

We are satisfied that archived electronic records reasonably capable of containing information within scope were considered as part of the searches undertaken. Any data stored within a system or database pre-dating the existing Collections Management Systems, would have been migrated into the incumbent solution, and therefore included in the search.

3. Correspondence and administrative records
The review considered whether correspondence or administrative records relating to the requested items were held.

The Museum's collections records include accession documentation and associated collection records relating to objects acquired by the Museum. Searches of those records did not identify any furniture, furnishings, antiques, fixtures, heirlooms or other movable property originating from Great House Farm.   As no such objects were identified as having been acquired by the Museum, no associated acquisition, provenance, ownership, loan, disposal or related correspondence concerning such objects was identified.

The review did not identify evidence that the Museum holds correspondence concerning the identification, ownership, recovery or location of Great House Farm furniture or household effects.

4. Search terms
We are satisfied that appropriate search terms and variants were used across the relevant collections management systems, collection records and associated documentation. These included relevant location names, property names, family names and associated variants reasonably capable of identifying records within scope.

The review is satisfied that the search methodology was reasonable and proportionate in the circumstances.

5. Transfer, disposal and destruction
The statement that the Museum is not aware of relevant records having been transferred or destroyed reflects the outcome of the searches undertaken and the knowledge of relevant collections staff.  The review did not identify any records showing that information within the scope of your request had been transferred to another institution or destroyed.

For clarity, the Museum's position is that no relevant records were identified.

6. Records concerning external institutions
We note that your request sought records concerning communications with Cardiff Council, Cardiff Castle, the Bute Estate and other bodies regarding objects originating from Great House Farm. Searches were not limited solely to object catalogue records. Relevant collection documentation and associated records were also considered.

No records were identified concerning furniture, furnishings, antiques, fixtures, heirlooms, or other movable property originating from Great House Farm, including correspondence with the organisations referred to in your request.

7. Advice and assistance
The Museum does not hold information identifying a specific department, collection, archive or record series within Cardiff Council or Cardiff Castle that is likely to contain the information you seek. The advice previously provided reflected our general view that those organisations would be more likely than Amgueddfa Cymru to hold records relating to the ownership, management or disposal of property associated with Great House Farm.

Conclusion
Having considered all of the information available, we are satisfied that Amgueddfa Cymru undertook reasonable and proportionate searches and that, on the balance of probabilities, the Museum does not hold recorded information falling within the scope of your request. The original decision is therefore upheld.

If you remain dissatisfied, you have the right to complain to the Information Commissioner's Office.



Cofion cynnes,

a. a search of transfer/accession-out records;

b. a review of retention and disposal records;

records.transcript:
Dear FOI Team,

Thank you for the internal review outcome dated 8 September 2026.

I note that the review upholds the original decision. I do not, however,
consider that the review has answered the substantive questions raised in
my request for internal review.

I am therefore putting the position on record, while also making a separate
new request for recorded information which your review confirms already
exists.

1. Records identified during the additional searches

On 14 August 2026, Amgueddfa Cymru stated that the additional enquiries had
identified:

"some information relating generally to Great House Farm and the
surrounding area".

The internal review now describes these as:

"a small number of records referring generally to Great House Farm,
Llandough".

The wording has therefore changed slightly, but the material fact has not:
the Museum confirms that records referring to Great House Farm were
identified.

My internal-review request specifically asked for those records to be
identified and, where not exempt, provided.

The review does not do so.

Simply stating that the records are considered to fall outside categories 1
to 9 does not identify what they are, where they are held, when they were
created, or their reference numbers.

2. Archived electronic systems

My request of 14 August specifically asked:

- which archived systems were searched;
- the approximate date ranges covered;
- whether historical email or correspondence archives were searched;
- whether legacy collections-management databases were searched; and
- whether any archived systems were unavailable, incomplete or incapable of
being searched.

The review answers none of these questions individually.

Instead, it states:

"archived electronic records reasonably capable of containing information
within scope were considered"

and:

"Any data stored within a system or database pre-dating the existing
Collections Management Systems, would have been migrated into the incumbent
solution, and therefore included in the search."

The first statement describes a conclusion, rather than identifying the
systems actually searched.

The second is an assumption about migration completeness. "Would have been
migrated" is not a search result and does not establish that the relevant
historical data was in fact migrated, completely migrated, retained,
searchable and included in the particular search undertaken.

3. Correspondence independent of accessioned objects

This is the most significant issue.

The original request expressly sought correspondence and administrative
records concerning, among other things:

- identification;
- recovery;
- ownership;
- location;
- the Buckler and Williams families;
- Cardiff Council;
- Cardiff Castle;
- the Bute Estate;
- museums; and
- other public authorities.

Those categories were deliberately not restricted to objects which had
subsequently been accessioned by the Museum.

The review states:

"As no such objects were identified as having been acquired by the Museum,
no associated acquisition, provenance, ownership, loan, disposal or related
correspondence concerning such objects was identified."

That reasoning addresses correspondence attached to an identified
accessioned object. It does not establish that correspondence was searched
for independently of an accession record.

For example, an enquiry concerning an item, a communication about possible
provenance, a request to identify an object, a discussion concerning
temporary custody, a disposal enquiry, a communication with another
institution, or correspondence about the contents of a property could exist
without the item ever becoming an accessioned Museum object.

Accordingly, the fact that no accessioned object was identified does not
itself establish that no such correspondence existed or was held.

The subsequent statement:

"The review did not identify evidence that the Museum holds correspondence
concerning the identification, ownership, recovery or location of Great
House Farm furniture or household effects."

still does not establish whether the relevant correspondence repositories
were actually searched.

4. Search terms

My internal-review request set out specific terms and variants and asked
the Museum to confirm whether those terms had been used.

The review now states only:

"appropriate search terms and variants were used"

and refers generally to:

"location names, property names, family names and associated variants".

That does not confirm whether the specific terms identified in my request
were searched.

In particular, the review does not say whether searches included
combinations or variants involving:

"Bute Estate", "Bute", "Cardiff Castle", "Cardiff Council", "household
effects", "contents", "dispersal", "recovery", "transfer", "demolition",
"provenance", "ownership"

and the other terms specifically identified in my 14 August correspondence.

The distinction matters because a search for a property name or family name
is not necessarily equivalent to a search for correspondence concerning the
dispersal, recovery, transfer or ownership of its contents.

5. Transfer, disposal and destruction

My request also asked what evidential basis existed for the earlier
statement that the Museum was not aware of relevant records having been
transferred to another institution or destroyed.

The review now █████:

"The statement that the Museum is not aware of relevant records having been
transferred or destroyed reflects the outcome of the searches undertaken
and the knowledge of relevant collections staff."

This combines two different things: documentary searches and institutional
█████.

It does not tell me whether the Museum searched:

- transfer or accession-out records;
- disposal records;
- retention and destruction records;
- archival transfer documentation; or
- other records capable of establishing whether material had previously
been transferred or destroyed.

There is an important distinction between:

"no record of transfer or destruction was identified in the records
searched"

and:

"there is no evidence that any transfer or destruction occurred".

The review does not make that distinction sufficiently clear.

6. Searches concerning external institutions

The original request expressly contemplated records concerning Cardiff
Council, Cardiff Castle, the Bute Estate and other external bodies.

The review states:

"Searches were not limited solely to object catalogue records."

That is helpful, but it still does not identify what non-catalogue
repositories were searched.

For example, it does not identify whether searches were made of curator
correspondence, departmental files, donor correspondence,
acquisition/disposal correspondence, provenance files, loan files,
institutional correspondence indexes, or other historical administrative
records in which communications with external institutions might have been
recorded.

Again, the issue is not whether the Museum considers the search reasonable.
It is whether the relevant classes of records were actually searched.

7. The significance of the "balance of probabilities" conclusion

I note the review's conclusion that, "on the balance of probabilities", the
Museum does not hold recorded information within the scope of the request.

I do not dispute that a negative FOI determination may ultimately be
reached on that basis.

However, the balance-of-probabilities conclusion necessarily depends upon
the quality, scope and rigour of the searches on which it is based. The
ICO's guidance states that, where a requester disputes whether relevant
information has been located, the authority should be able to provide a
reasoned and detailed account of how it determined that further information
was not held, including the areas searched, staff consulted and, for
electronic searches, the keywords, accounts and time parameters used.

My concern remains that the review repeatedly substitutes statements such
as "we are satisfied", "appropriate", "reasonably capable" and "on the
balance of probabilities" for the underlying factual information about what
was actually searched.

I therefore consider the review outcome insufficiently informative on the
specific search methodology raised in my review request.

I reserve my right to refer the handling of FOI 2026-020 and the internal
review to the Information Commissioner's Office.

Separate new FOI request

Separately from the above, I am now making a new request under the Freedom
of Information Act 2000.

This new request is deliberately limited to recorded information which your
own correspondence confirms was identified or generated in connection with
the searches already undertaken.

Please provide:

A. Records identified

The "small number of records referring generally to Great House Farm,
Llandough" identified during the additional enquiries referred to in your
email of 14 August 2026 and the internal review outcome of 8 September 2026.

For each record, please provide, where recorded:

- title or description;
- date;
- collection, series or department;
- system or repository;
- reference, accession or record number; and
- a copy of the record, subject to any applicable exemption.

If any part of a record is exempt, please identify the exemption relied
upon and provide the remainder where reasonably practicable.

Limb A is confined to the records your 14 August and 8 September letters
say were identified in the FOI 2026-020 additional enquiries. It is not a
new collection-wide search. If any of those records are also in scope of
FOI 2026-032 or FOI 2026-036, please schedule them once and cross-refer.
Please do not refuse this request as a duplicate.

B. Existing search records

Any recorded information already held concerning the searches undertaken
for FOI 2026-020 or its internal review, including any existing:

- search notes;
- search logs;
- search checklists;
- system lists;
- search-term lists;
- IT tickets or instructions;
- archived-system enquiries;
- staff search records; or
- other contemporaneous records documenting the searches undertaken.

I am asking only for recorded information already held. I am not asking the
Museum to create a new narrative or retrospective report.

If no such search records are held, please state that expressly.

Please register this as a new FOI request and provide it with its own
reference number. It is not a further internal review of FOI 2026-020, nor
is it a request to reopen or amend FOI 2026-032 or FOI 2026-036.

I would therefore be grateful if this request could be processed separately
and not treated as a clarification or continuation of those matters.

Regards,

Requester

Subject: Great House Farm, Llandough, Cardiff

National Monuments Record / FOI Officer,

This is a request under the Freedom of Information Act 2000 and, so far as the records concern the historic environment, the Environmental Information Regulations 2004.

I request copies of recorded information held by RCAHMW / the National Monuments Record of Wales relating to a reported discovery of ironwork or “armour” under the rear wing of Great House Farm (Ty Mawr), Llandough, Vale of Glamorgan (approx. ST 1681 7331; SMR / HER GGAT02038s; NMR NPRN associated with Great House Farm).

The published citations which identify RCAHMW as the source, and which state that the objects are at the National Museum of Wales, are:

1. RCAHMW, December 1988 — “Unpublished Records relating to Great House Farm prepared by R F Suggett, December 1988.” This is the source cited in the Glamorgan-Gwent Archaeological Trust assessment lodged on planning application 89/01396/OUT (and carried into 92/00671/RES):

   “it is likely that some medieval ironwork which is held by the National Museum of Wales was discovered under the rear wing c 1880 (RCAHMW 1988).”

   Bibliography: RCAHMW 1988 = Unpublished Records relating to Great House Farm prepared by R F Suggett, December 1988.
   (GGAT, Land at Great House Farm, Llandough: An Archaeological Assessment, August 1990.)

2. The same statement is repeated in Holbrook & Thomas, “An Early-medieval Monastic Cemetery at Llandough, Glamorgan”, Medieval Archaeology 49 (2005), p. 70 n. 142:

   “Mention should also be made of the fact that medieval ironwork was discovered under the rear wing of Great House Farm c. 1880. It is now in the collections of the National Museums & Galleries of Wales.”

3. The Heneb / Archwilio HER entry for Great House Farm (GGAT02038s) records armour / medieval ironwork found under the rear-wing floor c.1880 and attributes the note to RCAHMW.

Please therefore provide:

A. The full text of R F Suggett’s December 1988 unpublished records relating to Great House Farm, including every page or card that mentions ironwork, armour, a visor, a lance, a helmet, a burial, a soldier, a horse, a museum, or a find under the floor or rear wing / dairy.

B. Any earlier NMR / RCAHMW survey notes, correspondence or drawings that Suggett was using (including H. J. Thomas’s 1974 survey of the house, updated December 1988), insofar as they mention the c.1880 find or the destination of the objects.

C. Any record of the source of Suggett’s statement that the ironwork “is held by the National Museum of Wales” — for example a letter, accession note, conversation record, or museum catalogue reference.

D. Any later NMR / Coflein / correspondence file that confirms, corrects or withdraws that museum attribution.

E. File references, NPRNs and any copy letters sent to or received from the National Museum of Wales / Amgueddfa Cymru, GGAT, Cadw or the Vale of Glamorgan concerning this find.

I am not asking for advice or for a new interpretation. I am asking for the recorded information that underpins the 1988 sentence now cited as fact in the planning file and in Medieval Archaeology.

Please supply electronic copies where held. If any item is already published on Coflein, a catalogue link and reference is enough.

Regards,

Requester

records.transcript:
Councillor Burnett,

I write to you as Leader of the Vale of Glamorgan Council because the
elected member for Llandough, Councillor George D. D. Carroll, has not
answered a sequence of written enquiries spanning more than six months. I
am going above him for that reason alone. I am not asking you to adjudicate
the historic title dispute. I am asking that a constituent with a
documented family interest in the ward receive a reply that the ward member
has declined to give.

I understand that elected members do not have a line manager in the
employment sense. Councillor Carroll is Leader of the Conservative Group.
You are the political head of the authority. After the ward member and the
Monitoring Officer, you are the proper next addressee.

Why I am writing to you rather than waiting further

1. Councillor Carroll has not sent a single substantive reply to me at
█████.
2. On 27 July 2026 I filed a formal complaint about that silence (copied to
him, Democratic Services and the Monitoring Officer).
3. On 12 August 2026 Victoria Davidson, Monitoring Officer, wrote that the
matter fell outside the Corporate Concerns and Complaints Policy and that
she had not identified a Code of Conduct breach. That determination did not
require him to respond. It left the original questions unanswered.
4. I followed up with the Monitoring Officer on 12 August, 21 August and 24
August 2026. The position did not change.
5. I copied Councillor Carroll again on 28 August 2026 (joint letter with
Stephen Doughty MP). Still no reply from him.

The questions he has not answered include a simple, current, ward-level
one: who removed the tree my great-grandfather planted to mark the family’s
claim, as recorded in the Collection of Wales / archival image. That is a
local enquiry a ward member can signpost to Parks, Highways, Planning or
the landowner. It is not a request that he retry BP Properties Ltd v
Buckler.

From his public output, Councillor Carroll appears to concentrate on
blocked drains, potholes and similar highway defects. Those matters matter.
The correspondence I sent him is of a different character: heritage,
planning and enforcement records, the 1988 demolition of Great House Farm
(Ty Mawr), now Church View Close, and the removal of a commemorative tree.
I accept that may be outside the type of casework he usually handles. That
is why a short, honest reply — even if only to say the questions sit with
named officers, and to pass the tree query to the correct department —
would have been sufficient. Silence is not.

Recorded approaches to Councillor Carroll (█████)

All sent. No substantive reply on any of them.

- 16 February 2026 — “Title █████ and Procedural Concealment – Church View
Close, Llandough (formerly Great House Farm / Ty Mawr)”. Planning and
record-keeping gaps; 1988 demolition.
- 4 May 2026 — follow-up on BP v Buckler 1987; ITV footage; request for
attention as Llandough councillor.
- 3 May 2026 — joined the public “George Carroll for Llandough” Facebook
group (approved). Not a substitute for a council-email reply.
- 9 May 2026 — a wider formal notice also addressed to
█████. That address bounced. Subsequent mail used
the correct gdcarroll@ address.
- 7 June 2026 — “Church View Close, Llandough”. 1988 events from public
records, family █████ and media.
- 25 June 2026 — “Great House Farm, Llandough”. Asked whether he had
reviewed the earlier concerns and whether any discussion was possible.
- 13 July 2026 — “Great House Farm / Church View Close”. Full timeline
restated. Ten-working-day request. Explicit question: who removed the tree
my great-grandfather planted to commemorate the ownership claim, as shown
in the Collection of Wales archive image.
- 27 July 2026 — formal complaint to █████,
copied to Councillor Carroll, Democratic Services and the Monitoring
Officer.
- 28 August 2026 — further letter to Councillor Carroll and Stephen Doughty
MP on the same site.

What I am asking you to do

1. Note that the ward member has not answered, and that the complaint
process produced no requirement that he do so.

2. Ask Councillor Carroll, or the relevant Director, to provide a short
written reply on the tree: which department or landowner authorised or
carried out its removal, on what date, and under what power or works order
— or to confirm that the Council holds no such record.

3. Identify the correct officer contact for heritage, trees and historic
planning records at Church View Close / former Great House Farm, so I am
not left circling a silent ward inbox.

4. Confirm whether the Council will treat a documented family connection to
a demolished historic farmstead in the ward as a legitimate basis for a
reply, even where the correspondent is not presently resident in Llandough.

The thesis of my concern is that the lawfare/ warfare that systematically
attempted to make our occupancy permissive as early as the 40's (with my
grandmothers statement of title being █████, a failed attempt to get us
into a tenancy afterwards, and ambiguity in a 1955 order for another parcel
we leased and defaulted on, which later meant it was able to be
misinterpreted to make it appear our parcel of land (now Church View Close)
was part of theirs, like it was in 1916 - 1928) is a racket. The ownership
dispute was a problem created. The reaction followed and the solution was
to focus on possession. And so in 1987 BP were awarded possession with what
was a defective title chain.

I do not expect you to reopen 1987 litigation. I do expect the authority,
once the ward member has been given months and a formal complaint, to
answer a factual question about a tree on land in that ward. Because that
tree was part of a long list of evidence supporting our ownership claim.

I can supply the original emails and the 27 July complaint in full if
Democratic Services does not already have them. See attached the
aforementioned tree planting ceremy image. I also enclose a draft chancery
court allocation so you can understand the legal arguments.

Due to a lot of suspicious and conveniently timed deaths in our family,
surrounding this case, like my grandmother dying in the 2 weeks she will
have had to challenge BP quietly registering our land parcel in their names
in 1983, without declaring our ownership claim, which was never
exstinguished as the first 1974 court case was ajourned. Or my fathers
death after his appeal of the 1987 ruling was dismissed on grounds of
"heads BP win, tails we lose". Followed by ECHR rejection citing BP own the
land, despite BP only seeking possession and never seeking or gaining
ownership.

I have a trove of evidence and I am collecting more and investigating and
in talks with CPS and █████ Police and MoJ and Land Registry. The initial
thing I would like from you is the record of the removal of the tree we
planted. The picture attached depicts its location. I'd like to know who
removed it and when it was removed?

Regards,

Requester

I have been liaising a lot with local authorities in South Wales the last

or alternative lease arrangement for Lavernock Battery and Fort.

I understand that management and ownership of the site involve multiple
stakeholders, and I am reaching out to gauge your initial interest in such
an arrangement.

This proposal is a scenario that solves a common issue for this heritage
and coastal site—preventing dereliction, vandalism, and weathering through
active, professional occupation.

Rather than a traditional commercial takeover, the type of agreement would
have a responsible custodians on site. Guardianship tenancies are not new
to Councils in Wales.

deter anti-social behavior and immediately flag structural or environmental
issues.

low-impact, fully reversible, and designed to protect the historical
integrity of the architecture.

Nature Reserve and local businesses. Small team to operate quietly,
ensuring zero disruption to local wildlife, public footpaths, or
neighboring holiday operations.

I believe that breathing new life into these historic structures through a
controlled, professional occupancy could be an excellent model for
sustainable heritage preservation.

business associates, to see if a mutual arrangement could be reached. Could

Dear Requester

Thank you for your request for information about Llandough Primary School and your further enquires around whom you within the Information Governance team you have been corresponding with.

You asked

Under the Freedom of Information Act 2000 and, where applicable, the Environmental Information Regulations 2004, I request copies of records relating to the acquisition of the land used for the construction of Llandough Primary School.

Specifically, I request:

■ The transfer deed, conveyance or other legal instrument by which the Council acquired the land.

■ The purchase price or consideration paid for the land.

■ If the land was gifted, transferred at nominal value or below market value, records explaining the basis for that arrangement.

■ Any valuation reports obtained before acquisition.

■ Any agreements, correspondence or meeting minutes between the Council and BP (or any BP subsidiary, trust or associated company) concerning the transfer of the land.

■ Any Cabinet, Committee or Council reports authorising the acquisition.

■ Any planning agreements or obligations connected with the transfer.

If any of the requested information is already publicly available, please provide the relevant links or document references.

You then issued further correspondence requesting:

On 14 July 2026 you acknowledged my FOI/EIR request (Case Ref 00211027) concerning the acquisition of land for Llandough Primary School.

I replied the same day asking for the name of the officer who sent the acknowledgement. I have received no further response or substantive reply.

Our Response

The transfer deed, conveyance or other legal instrument by which the Council acquired the land
The Council holds a conveyance dated 11 June 1965 made between:
1.            Lakeside and Llandough Development Company Limited;
2.            Western Ground Rents Limited; and
3.            The Glamorgan County Council.
A scanned copy of the conveyance and its plan is attached (“the 1965 Conveyance”).

The purchase price or consideration paid for the land
The consideration recorded in the 1965 Conveyance is £16,800.

If the land was gifted, transferred at nominal value or below market value, records explaining the basis of that arrangement
The 1965 Conveyance records a purchase for £16,800. No record has been located within the papers held by Legal Services indicating that the land was gifted or transferred at nominal value or below market value.

Any valuation reports obtained before acquisition
Searches were undertaken with Legal Services and Estates Department. No valuation report relating to the acquisition has been identified. The Council does not hold any valuation report falling within the scope of this request.

Any agreements, correspondence or meeting minutes between the Council and BP, or any BP subsidiary, trust or associated company, concerning the transfer
No agreements, correspondence or meeting minutes between the Council and BP or any BP subsidiary, trust or associated company relating to the acquisition of the land have been identified.

Any Cabinet, Committee or Council reports authorising the acquisition
The Council has not identified any Cabinet, Committee or Council reports within its current records management systems which fall within the scope of your request. Given the age of the acquisition, any surviving historic records may have been transferred to Glamorgan Archives. You may wish to contact Glamorgan Archives directly regarding records from this period.

Any planning agreements or obligations connected with the transfer
No planning agreement or planning obligation connected with the 1965 Conveyance has been identified within the title deeds held by Legal Services or, within the Planning Departments records.

We have considered this aspect of your correspondence under the Freedom of Information Act 2000.
The Council’s Information Governance Team deal with requests on a collective basis and all requests will be considered by different officers. The requests are dealt with via a generic e-mail account so that all officers in the Team can consider correspondence.  There are several reasons why the Information Governance Team work in this way.  One reason is to ensure that correspondence is considered as soon as possible and to ensure that messages or e-mails are not sent to individuals and overlooked within our systems overall.  The information requested is also considered to constitute the personal data of a member of staff and disclosure would amount to disclosure to the world at large. Therefore the Council is unable to provide the name of the individual officer, because it is not considered that there is a lawful basis that would make disclosure fair or necessary in the circumstances.  The Council's correspondence is issued on behalf of the authority, and requests for information under the Freedom of Information Act 2000 or the Environmental Information Regulations 2004 are made to the Council as a public authority rather than to individual officers. 1. Ty Mawr / Great House, Bonvilston – still standing, Grade II (Cadw
13603), south side of the A48 opposite St Mary’s Church.

2. Great House Farm, Llandough (near Penarth) – NPRN 20182, ST1681073310,
demolished 6 December 1988. RCAHMW already holds NMR Site Files for it

surviving Bonvilston house. Adjacent ERC case RCS2/1/1776 is also of that
period.

Could you confirm from the location plan / map copies / photographs in the
RCS2/1/1777 bundle whether the site is Bonvilston (A48 / church opposite)

Royal Commission,

I am researching the demolition of Great House Farm (Tŷ Mawr),
Llandough-juxta-Penarth, in December 1988 (HER reference GGAT02038s / ST
1681 7331).

I am seeking to establish whether the Royal Commission was consulted or
notified before the farmhouse was demolished.

Contemporary reports from 3 December 1988 state that Cadw was considering
emergency protection/listing of Great House Farm and that a Cadw inspection
was being arranged, including discussion with the Royal Commission for
Ancient and Historical Monuments.

The farmhouse was then demolished on 6 December 1988.

I understand that the statutory framework at the time included provisions
concerning the recording of historic buildings before authorised
demolition. I would therefore be grateful if you could check your records
and confirm:

   1.

   Whether the Royal Commission received any notification, consultation,
   referral or request for advice concerning Great House Farm before its
   demolition in December 1988.
   2.

   Whether the Royal Commission was asked to inspect, photograph, record or
   otherwise document the building before demolition.
   3.

   Whether any correspondence exists between the Royal Commission, Cadw,
   the local planning authority, BP Properties Ltd, or their representatives
   concerning the proposed demolition.
   4.

   Whether the Royal Commission was given an opportunity to complete or
   supplement its earlier recording of the farmhouse before demolition.
   5.

   Whether your records contain any photographs, measured drawings,
   reports, field notes or other documentation relating specifically to the
   farmhouse immediately before its demolition.
   6.

   If records exist, I would be grateful for the relevant reference numbers
   and, where possible, copies.

For context, the Royal Commission had already recorded Great House Farm
architecturally in 1974. Contemporary material indicates that the building
was subsequently under consideration for emergency listing shortly before
its destruction.

There is also an important chronology concerning the occupation and
possession of the property: my late father William Buckler had lodged
European Commission of Human Rights application 14464/88 on 3 May 1988; BP
obtained possession on 29 November 1988; demolition began on 6 December
1988; and the Strasbourg application was registered on 12 December 1988.

I am not asking the Royal Commission to express an opinion on the ownership
dispute or the legality of the demolition. I am simply seeking to
establish, from your records, whether the Commission was notified or
consulted and what opportunity, if any, it was given to record the building
(our home since 1667) before it was destroyed?

Given the historical and archaeological significance subsequently
identified at the site, I would particularly appreciate confirmation of
whether any pre-demolition recording was requested or undertaken.

Regards


,


Requester

records.transcript:
Customer Relations / Planning Complaints Officer,

I wish to make a formal complaint concerning the Vale of Glamorgan
Council's Dear Customer Relations / Planning Complaints Officer,

I wish to make a formal complaint concerning the Vale of Glamorgan
Council's handling of Great House Farm, Llandough-juxta-Penarth,
particularly the circumstances surrounding its demolition in December 1988
and the subsequent planning process.


Please register this as a formal complaint under the Council's corporate
complaints procedure and provide me with a complaint reference number.


This complaint concerns the Council's administration and exercise of its
planning and heritage responsibilities. It is not intended to constitute an
appeal against a properly made historic planning decision.


1. Great House Farm, Llandough (Cardiff not Cowbridge) was recognised as a
building of historic importance


The planning and archaeological documentation concerning the site
identifies Great House Farm as a building of heritage significance.


In particular, the archaeological material identifies the former building
as a "county treasure" associated with SMR 2038s, while earlier
architectural recording by RCAHMW describes a substantial historic
farmhouse with surviving historic fabric.


The later 1990 archaeological assessment states:


«"Owing to an ownership dispute and the subsequent sudden destruction of
the property in 1988 the building was incompletely understood."»


I regard that statement as highly significant because it records,
contemporaneously with the subsequent planning process, that the building
had been destroyed suddenly and that its archaeological and architectural
history had therefore not been adequately understood or recorded.


2. The Council's apparent failure to take protective action before the 1988
demolition


I ask the Council to investigate what action, if any, its planning and
heritage officers took when Great House Farm was at risk of demolition.


In particular, I ask the Council to establish:


1. Whether the Council knew that Great House Farm was at risk of demolition
before December 1988.

2. Whether the Council received any notification, complaint, application,
correspondence or other warning concerning the proposed demolition.

3. Whether the building had been considered for statutory listing or other
statutory protection.

4. Whether consideration was given to the use of a Building Preservation
Notice or any other available statutory or administrative mechanism capable
of preventing or delaying demolition pending assessment.

5. Whether the Council's heritage officers, planning officers or
archaeological advisers were consulted.

6. Whether any inspection or photographic/architectural record was
undertaken immediately before or after the demolition.

7. Why, given the building's recognised historic significance, the Council
did not secure a comprehensive standing-building record before the building
was lost.


I am not asserting at this stage that a particular statutory power
necessarily had to be exercised. I am asking the Council to investigate
what powers and procedures were available in 1988 and why they were, or
were not, used in this case.


3. The "sudden destruction" of the building requires investigation


The 1990 archaeological assessment expressly attributes the incomplete
understanding of the building to its "subsequent sudden destruction ... in
1988".


I therefore ask the Council to establish from its records:


- the date on which it first became aware of the proposed or actual
demolition;

- the identity of the relevant officers;

- whether the Council received complaints or reports concerning demolition
activity;

- whether any site visit took place;

- whether any notice, warning, enforcement action, preservation action or
other intervention was considered;

- and whether the Council has retained records explaining why the
demolition was allowed to proceed.


This is particularly important because the building was subsequently
treated within the planning process as an already-cleared site.


4. The 1989 planning application appears to contain a significant
historical discrepancy


The outline planning application submitted by BP Properties Ltd in 1989
states, in the section asking which buildings were to be demolished:


«"None."»


The same application describes the site as "Disused" and the previous use
as "Not known".


This requires explanation because the application followed the demolition
of Great House Farm in December 1988 by approximately one year.


I ask the Council to investigate whether its planning officers:


- were aware of the former Great House Farm building when the 1989
application was processed;

- knew when and how it had been demolished;

- checked the accuracy of the applicant's statement that no buildings were
to be demolished;

- identified the former farmhouse in the planning history and supporting
documentation;

- and considered whether the demolition itself raised any planning,
heritage or enforcement issue requiring investigation.


I am particularly concerned that the planning process appears to have
proceeded on the basis of a cleared site without first establishing the
circumstances in which the historic building had disappeared.


5. Failure to create an adequate record of the lost building


The subsequent archaeological documentation states that the building was
"incompletely understood".


I ask the Council to explain what mitigation, recording or investigation it
required in consequence.


The documentary evidence presently available indicates that substantial
historic fabric and multiple phases of the building existed, yet the
building was destroyed without a complete standing-building survey having
been secured.


I therefore ask the Council to identify:


- all surveys undertaken before demolition;

- all surveys undertaken after demolition;

- all archaeological or architectural advice obtained by the Council;

- all photographs held by the Council;

- all correspondence concerning the building's architectural or historic
importance;

- and the Council's policy or practice in 1988 concerning the recording of
significant unlisted historic buildings at risk.


6. Subsequent planning treatment of the site


Following demolition, the planning process concentrated heavily on
below-ground archaeology, ultimately resulting in archaeological
investigation of the cemetery and associated remains.


I do not suggest that archaeological excavation was inappropriate. My
concern is that the destruction of the standing historic building appears
to have been treated as a fait accompli rather than as an event requiring
accountability and an explanation of how the Council's heritage
responsibilities had been discharged.


The later planning documentation should therefore be reviewed alongside the
records relating to the 1988 demolition.


In particular, I ask the Council to identify precisely when the planning
authority first recorded the former farmhouse as demolished and what
explanation was placed on the planning file for its loss.


7. Matters I ask the Council to investigate


Please investigate and provide a substantive response to the following
questions:


A. What did Vale of Glamorgan Council know about the impending demolition
of Great House Farm before December 1988?


B. What statutory and non-statutory heritage protections were available to
the Council at the time?


C. Were any of those mechanisms considered or discussed?


D. Were any Building Preservation Notice, listing, enforcement, urgent
works, archaeological recording or other protective measures considered?


E. Why was the building apparently destroyed without a comprehensive
standing-building survey?


F. What records does the Council hold concerning the demolition itself?


G. Why did the 1989 planning application proceed despite the recent
demolition of a building identified in the archaeological record as a
"county treasure"?


H. Why was the applicant's answer "None" given to the question concerning
buildings to be demolished, and did the Council investigate the apparent
discrepancy?


I. Did any Council officer consider whether the 1988 demolition constituted
a breach of planning control or otherwise required investigation?


J. Did the Council investigate whether the building had been demolished
lawfully?


K. What heritage assessment was undertaken before the subsequent
development permissions were processed?


L. What lessons has the Council subsequently incorporated into its
procedures for County Treasures and other locally significant historic
buildings?


8. Records requested as part of the investigation


Please preserve and review all relevant records, including planning files,
enforcement records, heritage files, committee papers, officer reports,
internal correspondence, site inspection notes, photographs, archaeological
correspondence and consultation records concerning:


- Great House Farm / Tŷ Mawr / Cedfin / Cydfin;

- SMR/HER reference 2038s / GGAT02038s;

- the December 1988 demolition;

- the 1989 outline planning application;

- the 1990 archaeological assessment;

- and the subsequent reserved matters/development applications.


I would also ask that the Council identify any material which has been
destroyed or cannot now be located, together with the applicable
retention/disposal record where one exists.


9. Outcome sought


I am seeking a formal investigation and a reasoned written explanation of
the Council's actions and omissions.


In particular, I ask the Council to determine:


1. Whether its officers discharged the heritage and planning
responsibilities applicable at the time.

2. Whether any failure occurred in relation to the identification,
protection, recording or investigation of Great House Farm.

3. Whether the Council's handling of the 1989 planning application
appropriately addressed the recent demolition of the building.

4. Whether any relevant records have been lost or destroyed and, if so,

need to be dealt with separately under the appropriate information-access

Requester of Great House Farm, Llandough-juxta-Penarth, particularly the
circumstances surrounding its demolition in December 1988 and the
subsequent planning process.

Please register this as a formal complaint under the Council's corporate
complaints procedure and provide me with a complaint reference number.

This complaint concerns the Council's administration and exercise of its
planning and heritage responsibilities. It is not intended to constitute an
appeal against a properly made historic planning decision.
1. Great House Farm was recognised as a building of historic importance

The planning and archaeological documentation concerning the site
identifies Great House Farm as a building of heritage significance.

In particular, the archaeological material identifies the former building
as a "county treasure" associated with SMR 2038s, while earlier
architectural recording by RCAHMW describes a substantial historic
farmhouse with surviving historic fabric.

The later 1990 archaeological assessment states:

"Owing to an ownership dispute and the subsequent sudden destruction of the
property in 1988 the building was incompletely understood."

I regard that statement as highly significant because it records,
contemporaneously with the subsequent planning process, that the building
had been destroyed suddenly and that its archaeological and architectural
history had therefore not been adequately understood or recorded.
2. The Council's apparent failure to take protective action before the 1988
demolition

I ask the Council to investigate what action, if any, its planning and
heritage officers took when Great House Farm was at risk of demolition.

In particular, I ask the Council to establish:

   1. Whether the Council knew that Great House Farm was at risk of
   demolition before December 1988.
   2. Whether the Council received any notification, complaint,
   application, correspondence or other warning concerning the proposed
   demolition.
   3. Whether the building had been considered for statutory listing or
   other statutory protection.
   4. Whether consideration was given to the use of a Building Preservation
   Notice or any other available statutory or administrative mechanism capable
   of preventing or delaying demolition pending assessment.
   5. Whether the Council's heritage officers, planning officers or
   archaeological advisers were consulted.
   6. Whether any inspection or photographic/architectural record was
   undertaken immediately before or after the demolition.
   7. Why, given the building's recognised historic significance, the
   Council did not secure a comprehensive standing-building record before the
   building was lost.

I am not asserting at this stage that a particular statutory power
necessarily had to be exercised. I am asking the Council to investigate
what powers and procedures were available in 1988 and why they were, or
were not, used in this case.
3. The "sudden destruction" of the building requires investigation

The 1990 archaeological assessment expressly attributes the incomplete
understanding of the building to its "subsequent sudden destruction ... in
1988".

I therefore ask the Council to establish from its records:

   - the date on which it first became aware of the proposed or actual
   demolition;
   - the identity of the relevant officers;
   - whether the Council received complaints or reports concerning
   demolition activity;
   - whether any site visit took place;
   - whether any notice, warning, enforcement action, preservation action
   or other intervention was considered;
   - and whether the Council has retained records explaining why the
   demolition was allowed to proceed.

This is particularly important because the building was subsequently
treated within the planning process as an already-cleared site.
4. The 1989 planning application appears to contain a significant
historical discrepancy

The outline planning application submitted by BP Properties Ltd in 1989
states, in the section asking which buildings were to be demolished:

"None."

The same application describes the site as "Disused" and the previous use
as "Not known".

This requires explanation because the application followed the demolition
of Great House Farm in December 1988 by approximately one year.

I ask the Council to investigate whether its planning officers:

   - were aware of the former Great House Farm building when the 1989
   application was processed;
   - knew when and how it had been demolished;
   - checked the accuracy of the applicant's statement that no buildings
   were to be demolished;
   - identified the former farmhouse in the planning history and supporting
   documentation;
   - and considered whether the demolition itself raised any planning,
   heritage or enforcement issue requiring investigation.

I am particularly concerned that the planning process appears to have
proceeded on the basis of a cleared site without first establishing the
circumstances in which the historic building had disappeared.
5. Failure to create an adequate record of the lost building

The subsequent archaeological documentation states that the building was
"incompletely understood".

I ask the Council to explain what mitigation, recording or investigation it
required in consequence.

The documentary evidence presently available indicates that substantial
historic fabric and multiple phases of the building existed, yet the
building was destroyed without a complete standing-building survey having
been secured.

I therefore ask the Council to identify:

   - all surveys undertaken before demolition;
   - all surveys undertaken after demolition;
   - all archaeological or architectural advice obtained by the Council;
   - all photographs held by the Council;
   - all correspondence concerning the building's architectural or historic
   importance;
   - and the Council's policy or practice in 1988 concerning the recording
   of significant unlisted historic buildings at risk.

6. Subsequent planning treatment of the site

Following demolition, the planning process concentrated heavily on
below-ground archaeology, ultimately resulting in archaeological
investigation of the cemetery and associated remains.

I do not suggest that archaeological excavation was inappropriate. My
concern is that the destruction of the standing historic building appears
to have been treated as a fait accompli rather than as an event requiring
accountability and an explanation of how the Council's heritage
responsibilities had been discharged.

The later planning documentation should therefore be reviewed alongside the
records relating to the 1988 demolition.

In particular, I ask the Council to identify precisely when the planning
authority first recorded the former farmhouse as demolished and what
explanation was placed on the planning file for its loss.
7. Matters I ask the Council to investigate

Please investigate and provide a substantive response to the following
questions:

A. What did Vale of Glamorgan Council know about the impending demolition
of Great House Farm before December 1988?

B. What statutory and non-statutory heritage protections were available to
the Council at the time?

C. Were any of those mechanisms considered or discussed?

D. Were any Building Preservation Notice, listing, enforcement, urgent
works, archaeological recording or other protective measures considered?

E. Why was the building apparently destroyed without a comprehensive
standing-building survey?

F. What records does the Council hold concerning the demolition itself?

G. Why did the 1989 planning application proceed despite the recent
demolition of a building identified in the archaeological record as a
"county treasure"?

H. Why was the applicant's answer "None" given to the question concerning
buildings to be demolished, and did the Council investigate the apparent
discrepancy?

I. Did any Council officer consider whether the 1988 demolition constituted
a breach of planning control or otherwise required investigation?

J. Did the Council investigate whether the building had been demolished
lawfully?

K. What heritage assessment was undertaken before the subsequent
development permissions were processed?

L. What lessons has the Council subsequently incorporated into its
procedures for County Treasures and other locally significant historic
buildings?
8. Records requested as part of the investigation

Please preserve and review all relevant records, including planning files,
enforcement records, heritage files, committee papers, officer reports,
internal correspondence, site inspection notes, photographs, archaeological
correspondence and consultation records concerning:

   - Great House Farm / Tŷ Mawr / Cedfin / Cydfin;
   - SMR/HER reference 2038s / GGAT02038s;
   - the December 1988 demolition;
   - the 1989 outline planning application;
   - the 1990 archaeological assessment;
   - and the subsequent reserved matters/development applications.

I would also ask that the Council identify any material which has been
destroyed or cannot now be located, together with the applicable
retention/disposal record where one exists.
9. Outcome sought

I am seeking a formal investigation and a reasoned written explanation of
the Council's actions and omissions.

In particular, I ask the Council to determine:

   1. Whether its officers discharged the heritage and planning
   responsibilities applicable at the time.
   2. Whether any failure occurred in relation to the identification,
   protection, recording or investigation of Great House Farm.
   3. Whether the Council's handling of the 1989 planning application
   appropriately addressed the recent demolition of the building.
   4. Whether any relevant records have been lost or destroyed and, if so,
   when and under what retention arrangements.
   5. What procedural lessons arise from the case.

I also request disclosure of the relevant non-exempt records identified
during the complaint investigation, where these are not otherwise
available. I recognise that requests for specific recorded information may
need to be dealt with separately under the appropriate information-access
regime.

I have only recently been able to examine and correlate the surviving
planning, archaeological and heritage documentation sufficiently to
identify these issues. I therefore ask that the Council accepts the
complaint for investigation notwithstanding the age of the events concerned.

Please acknowledge receipt and confirm the complaint reference and the
officer responsible for its investigation.

Yours faithfully,




Requester

Royal Commission,

I am researching the demolition of Great House Farm (Tŷ Mawr), Llandough-juxta-Penarth, in December 1988 (HER reference GGAT02038s / ST 1681 7331).

I am seeking to establish whether the Royal Commission was consulted or notified before the farmhouse was demolished.

Contemporary reports from 3 December 1988 state that Cadw was considering emergency protection/listing of Great House Farm and that a Cadw inspection was being arranged, including discussion with the Royal Commission for Ancient and Historical Monuments.

The farmhouse was then demolished on 6 December 1988.

I understand that the statutory framework at the time included provisions concerning the recording of historic buildings before authorised demolition. I would therefore be grateful if you could check your records and confirm:

  1.  Whether the Royal Commission received any notification, consultation, referral or request for advice concerning Great House Farm before its demolition in December 1988.
  2.  Whether the Royal Commission was asked to inspect, photograph, record or otherwise document the building before demolition.
  3.  Whether any correspondence exists between the Royal Commission, Cadw, the local planning authority, BP Properties Ltd, or their representatives concerning the proposed demolition.
  4.  Whether the Royal Commission was given an opportunity to complete or supplement its earlier recording of the farmhouse before demolition.
  5.  Whether your records contain any photographs, measured drawings, reports, field notes or other documentation relating specifically to the farmhouse immediately before its demolition.
  6.  If records exist, I would be grateful for the relevant reference numbers and, where possible, copies.

For context, the Royal Commission had already recorded Great House Farm architecturally in 1974. Contemporary material indicates that the building was subsequently under consideration for emergency listing shortly before its destruction.

There is also an important chronology concerning the occupation and possession of the property: my late father William Buckler had lodged European Commission of Human Rights application 14464/88 on 3 May 1988; BP obtained possession on 29 November 1988; demolition began on 6 December 1988; and the Strasbourg application was registered on 12 December 1988.

I am not asking the Royal Commission to express an opinion on the ownership dispute or the legality of the demolition. I am simply seeking to establish, from your records, whether the Commission was notified or consulted and what opportunity, if any, it was given to record the building (our home since 1667) before it was destroyed?

Given the historical and archaeological significance subsequently identified at the site, I would particularly appreciate confirmation of whether any pre-demolition recording was requested or undertaken.

Haidee,

Thanks.

I am also asking the Senedd to consider whether the circumstances
surrounding the demolition of Great House Farm, Llandough-juxta-Penarth,
and the subsequent planning and heritage history of the site warrant
independent scrutiny and, ultimately, a public inquiry or Senedd committee
inquiry.

I am not asking the Senedd to determine a private property dispute or to
decide legal questions that properly belong before the courts. My concern
is the conduct, decision-making, record-keeping and accountability of
public bodies responsible for heritage protection, planning and local
government.

The surviving evidence presents a series of unusually important questions.

Great House Farm was professionally surveyed by the Royal Commission on the
Ancient and Historical Monuments of Wales in 1974. In December 1988, Cadw
was considering the building for emergency spot-listing, with a
contemporary report stating that inspectors were due to visit and consider
the case. The European Commission of Human Rights records that the
Convention application had been introduced on 3 May 1988; BP obtained
possession on 29 November 1988; demolition began on 6 December 1988; and
the application was not registered by the Commission until 12 December 1988.

The evidence therefore establishes a very compressed sequence in which
emergency heritage protection was being considered, domestic interim relief
was refused, possession was obtained and the building was then destroyed
within days.

That chronology does not, by itself, establish coordination, deliberate
suppression or unlawful conduct. It does, however, warrant investigation.

There are several specific questions which I believe require answers from
an authority independent of the present local authority:

   1.

   What information and records were actually considered by Cadw when the
   1988 spot-listing decision was made?
   2.

   Was the 1974 RCAHMW architectural survey considered, and if not, why not?
   3.

   What communications took place between Cadw, South Glamorgan County
   Council, BP Properties Ltd, the courts and any other public bodies during
   the critical period immediately preceding demolition?
   4.

   What consideration was given by the local planning authority to the
   available statutory powers of preservation in circumstances where
   demolition was imminent?
   5.

   Why was the building destroyed before there could be an independent
   retrospective architectural examination of the fabric?
   6.

   How should the later archaeological evidence, including the discovery of
   approximately 1,026 burials in 1994, be understood in assessing the
   historic significance of the site and the adequacy of the earlier
   decision-making? I recognise that this later discovery cannot
   retrospectively prove that the 1988 listing decision was unlawful.
   7.

   A 1989 planning document appears to describe the site as having formerly
   contained Great House Farm “(a listed building)”. I ask that this apparent
   discrepancy be investigated and reconciled with the 1988 Cadw decision.
   8.

   What records relating to these decisions still exist, where are they
   held, and have reasonable steps been taken to preserve and disclose them?

I am particularly concerned that the destruction of the physical building
in December 1988 permanently removed primary architectural evidence which
could otherwise have been examined independently.

I also ask the Senedd to consider the wider public-interest question:
whether the present mechanisms for accountability are adequate where a
historic building is destroyed during a period of rapidly developing legal,
planning and heritage proceedings and significant questions remain about
what information was available to decision-makers.

I would therefore ask the Petitions Committee to consider accepting a
petition on this subject and, where appropriate, referring the matter to
the relevant Senedd committee or committees for investigation. I would also
welcome consideration of whether an independent public inquiry, committee
inquiry or other form of external investigation would be appropriate.

I am prepared to provide the underlying documents, chronology, court
material, heritage records, planning documents and correspondence
supporting these questions.

I am not asking the Senedd to adopt my conclusions. I am asking that the
evidence and unanswered questions be examined independently and that the
relevant public bodies be required to account for what they did, what they
knew, and what records exist.

Please confirm the appropriate route for submitting this formally to the
Senedd and whether the material can be referred to the Petitions Committee
for consideration.

Yours faithfully,

Requester

records.transcript:
Mr Wigley,

I am writing to make a *formal complaint to Cadw* concerning the handling
and substantive response to my correspondence regarding Great House Farm
(Tŷ Mawr), Llandough, and particularly Cadw's 1988 consideration of whether
the building should be protected by listing.

I am making this complaint directly to Cadw at this stage because I
consider that Cadw should be given a proper opportunity to review and
address the matters before any escalation to the wider Welsh Government
complaints process.

For the avoidance of doubt, I am *not making a further Freedom of
Information request* and I am not simply asking Cadw to produce records
which it has already said no longer exist. I accept that Cadw has stated
that all records it currently holds concerning the 1988 listing decision
have been released.

My complaint concerns what can properly be established from the surviving
evidence, whether the responses I have received have adequately addressed
that evidence, and whether the historical record can now be described
accurately where the underlying file has been lost.
1. The newly identified 1982 evidence

I have now identified a 1 October 1982 consultation letter from the
Glamorgan-Gwent Archaeological Trust concerning the East Vale Local Plan
and the proposed Ty Maw Farm site, identified as *H2.1*.

The letter states:

“Ty Maw Farm (H2.1) is designated as a three-acre residential site. As you
will see from the enclosed information the settlement at Llandough
developed considerably from farming and fishing... Recent excavations at
Llandough by the Trust revealed early occupation, part of the villa and
medieval grange buildings. There remains a possibility that occupation
continues to the north of the church; provision should be made, therefore,
for thorough investigative work prior to the development.”

I do not suggest that this document, by itself, establishes that the
standing farmhouse was required to be listed.

Its significance is narrower and more demonstrable: *six years before the
1988 demolition, the archaeological and planning system already contained
site-specific information identifying Ty Maw Farm as a proposed development
site and recording substantial archaeological sensitivity in the immediate
Llandough area, including possible continued occupation north of the
church.*

That materially affects the historical context in which Cadw's 1988

Under the Freedom of Information Act 2000 and/or the Environmental
Information Regulations 2004 (whichever regime the Council considers

   March 1990); and
   - The subsequent reserved matters application *92/00671/RES*,

subsequently developed as Church View Close.

record between the outline permission and the subsequent
detailed/reserved-matters approval.

The Council's own case officer's report on application 89/01396/OUT
records, in its consultations section:

"Cardiff Bay Development Corporation: No objections – however, the
Corporation would hope that the trees on the slope of the site facing
north-west are retained and that the public right of way which runs through
the site will be retained."

Rivers Authority* and the *County Engineer* by reference to attached typed
sheets ("please type attached sh②" and "please type attached sh③"), without
reproducing their substantive contents in the disclosed copy.

   1.

   The *complete original written response from the Cardiff Bay Development
   Corporation* concerning application 89/01396/OUT, including any
   accompanying letter, report, plan, attachment or other document forming
   part of that consultation response.
   2.

   The *complete National Rivers Authority consultation response* referred
   to in the report as one of the attached sheets, including the original
   document and any accompanying material.
   3.

   The *complete County Engineer consultation response* referred to in the
   report as one of the attached sheets, including the original document and
   any accompanying material.

and ③ to identify which sheet belongs to which consultee, as the numerals
are difficult to distinguish in the surviving copy. Please identify the
corresponding sheet/document by reference to its contents or file
provenance.

   showing when the NRA and County Engineer responses were received by the
   Council and how those responses were placed on, incorporated into or
   considered as part of the planning file.

   5.

   The *formal decision notice and complete schedule of conditions* issued
   in connection with planning application 89/01396/OUT, including any
   condition concerning archaeological investigation, evaluation, assessment,
   excavation, recording, preservation or protection.
   6.

   All records held by the Council demonstrating the *discharge,
   implementation or consideration of any archaeological condition*
   attached to the 1990 outline permission, including any archaeological
   evaluation, field assessment, report, correspondence, approval, discharge
   notice, consultation response or internal officer record.
   7.

   Any correspondence or documentation showing how the Council considered
   the findings of that archaeological work in determining the subsequent
   reserved matters application 92/00671/RES.

   8.

   The *formal decision notice* for application 92/00671/RES, including the
   complete schedule of any conditions attached to the approval.
   9.

   The consultation responses and representations received in connection
